doc.title: Panama Francis interviewed by Michael Woods, Los Angeles, California, September 1, 1995

title: Southern pay, prices and dressing like a musician
summary: A gig paid a dollar and a half, which bought plenty of food; musicians dressed the part, and he disapproves of sneakers on stage today.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Getting paid: wages, scale and the pay envelope

blocks.x: Tell us about how it was like, the travel, the pay, the lifestyle of working with the traveling band.

Now up until I went north, I mean the pay was low, because well in the south the salaries was low. Nobody was making no big bucks. So I mean the salaries was low. Like we got a dollar and a half a night for playing a gig. But with a dollar and a half, you can go to the store the next day and buy a dollar and a half worth of food.
What would a dollar and a half buy at that time?
Well you could get three pounds of fish for a dime.

You could get spare ribs or pork chops or steak for a quarter a pound. String beans and collard greens and all that, people used to throw that away. You know, so it was, a dollar and a half went a long way. Like room rent, people used to charge like three dollars a week for a room you know. And see there’s one thing I mean you see me like this now, I came up in this type of school. Where a musician looked the part of a musician. You didn’t dress like any and everybody. You stood out like a sore thumb in the crowd. Everybody knew who the musician was. Because he was the guy that was dressed. He had on a shirt and a tie. Like I used to change suits sometimes three times a day. I owned over thirty suits of clothes. But nowadays, it kind of bugs me to see a musician walk up on the bandstand with sneakers on and a sports shirt. Well, that’s the way it is today, but when I was coming up, you knew who the musician was. He didn’t look like any and everybody in the neighborhood.
